entries.title: Georgetown Takes Down Maryland For 86-74 Win
entries.summary: Jaland Lowe finished with 22 points and eight assists for the Hoyes, which made 15 3-pointers.
entries.content:
Jaland Lowe made 5 of 8 from 3-point range and finished with 22 points and eight assists Saturday night to help Georgetown beat Maryland 86-74.

Elmarko Jackson added 17 points and Kayvon Mulready scored 15 on five 3s for Georgetown (2-0). Vincent Iwuchukwu had 12 points.

Lowe and Mulready hit 3-pointers 24 seconds apart that made it 38-26 with 2:38 left in the first half and the Hoyas led by double figures the rest of the way.

Pharrel Payne had 28 points and eight assists while shooting 10 of 14 from the field and 8 of 8 from the free-throw line for Maryland (1-1). Freshman Kaden House scored all of his 13 points in the second half. DJ Wagner added 11 points.

The Hoyas made 15 3-pointers — the program’s most since in a single game since 2010 — on 30 attempts and shot 52% overall.

Mulready hit a 3 that capped a 12-3 opening run in the second half. Georgetown pushed its lead as high as 27 points and led by 22 with 2 minutes left.

Maryland, which closed the game on a 19-6 run, made 26 of 63 (41%) from the field and shot just 15% (3 of 20) from behind the arc.

Up Next

Maryland: Hosts No. 9 Virginia on Friday.

Georgetown: Hosts Delaware State on Tuesday.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Permitting Reform Is Heading Into a Key Vote With an Unsteady Coalition
entries.summary: The bipartisan bill received new support after weekend amendments. But with new wind under their sails, Democrats sound less willing to accept the deal.
entries.content:
Lawmakers behind a bipartisan permitting reform package released amendments to their bill this weekend ahead of a consequential procedural vote Monday. It’s not clear their changes went far enough to win over their critics.

The amendments seek to address concerns from environmental groups, Native American tribes and the utility industry. The bipartisan group of lawmakers struck a section that would have let the federal government take over the role of tribal historic preservation officers in some cases and strengthened some provisions around building transmission lines that could support a clean energy transition.

Among other changes, the amendment also adds a new “data center community assistance” program, which would offer local, state and tribal governments technical assistance on a proposed data center’s impacts on power, water, costs, jobs and taxes. The bill already included provisions that would force data center developers to pay more for power.

After the amendment was released Saturday, the advocacy group Evergreen Action joined other climate-solutions-focused organizations in endorsing the deal, saying it would enable a clean energy transition and keep down energy costs.

“These changes have been too long delayed, already. Despite the monumental election, I do not believe that a better deal is around the corner,” Lena Moffitt, the executive director of Evergreen Action, said in a statement.

But several groups said the amendment didn’t go far enough. The changes did not sway a coalition dedicated to the preservation of the National Historic Preservation Act that includes the National Congress of American Indians and the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers.

That coalition characterized the amendment as “lipstick on a pig.”

Major players like the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council also have not yet said whether their conditional opposition might turn into support.

The amendment comes before a major test of the unsteady coalition behind the bill. It remains unclear whether Democrats are willing to support a deal negotiated with Republican leaders and the White House after massive victories in the midterms that will shift the balance of power in Congress leftward after January.

The Trump administration and other Republicans have pushed for Congress to pass the bill, framing it as a fast-track for infrastructure development.

Bill sponsor Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) said the amendment “preserves the foundation” of the deal while making “targeted changes” based on stakeholder feedback.

“I’ve worked hard to incorporate the feedback we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into this Substitute Amendment,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico), another sponsor of the legislation.

In recent days, heavy-hitters like the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers and the North American Building Trades Union have come out in support of the legislation. But with the wind of Tuesday’s blue wave in their sails, some Democrats and environmental groups expressed their opposition, saying a better deal could come together with the balance of power in Congress shifting to the left.

Before the amendment was released, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the deal “falls short” on issues of Tribal sovereignty and environmental policy reform, and criticized the lack of input from House members. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) said Democrats should push for a better deal, as did Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), who opposed the package. On Saturday, a spokesperson for Wyden said the senator’s team “continue to have unresolved concerns.”

Reps. Melanie Stansbury (D-New Mexico) and Adelita Grijalva (D-Arizona) called for Senate leadership to “reconsider” Monday’s vote.

Stansbury and Grijalva said the bill, even with the amendment, would “undermine Tribal sovereignty and cultural rights, weaken protections for communities, the environment, public lands, clean water, and wildlife, and severely limit the ability of communities to have their voices heard in decisions that directly impact them.”

The changes weren’t enough to win over the All Pueblo Council of Governors, a group Heinrich has worked closely with in the past, which said they did not receive a draft of the amendment and haven’t been able to participate in the process. Several groups and lawmakers have expressed that concern as the permitting bill moves through Congress without any committee hearings.

The chair of the council, Joey Sanchez of Santa Ana Pueblo, said the process disrespected tribes and was an “affront to their sovereignty.”

"We are profoundly disappointed and frustrated," Sanchez said. "Despite the concerns we relayed, both the Tribes and the Public are still not part of the process, and APCG still have not been consulted."

Several groups said the amendments constituted improvements, but still fell short.

Abre' Conner, director of the NAACP's Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, told The Sun, "while some portions of the bill have improved, the bill's fundamental problems are still there.”

“It will still be harder to hold polluters accountable and core environmental laws remain weaker," Conner said.

The Coalition of Large Tribes, which proposed several changes to the bill that were incorporated into the amendment, said Saturday that the group was “grateful to see many positive changes,” but said there was “still room for improvement.”

The bill has received some support from Native American groups and Tribal leaders, particularly those with energy resources. Apsáalooke Nation/Crow Tribe chair Frank White Clay expressed support in a letter to the bill’s sponsors in late October, saying unpredictable permitting timelines have hindered investments.

“We appreciate your bipartisan leadership in addressing permitting barriers that limit economic opportunity for tribes with coal, oil and natural gas resources,” Clay wrote.

The National Tribal Energy Association sent a letter Thursday in support of provisions that “advance Tribal self-determination, streamline infrastructure deployment across Indian Country, and unlock Tribal energy potential.” And Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kansas), a citizen of the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin and the longest-serving Native woman in Congress, also came out in support of the permitting reform package Friday.

Big environmental nonprofits mainly hedged last month, noting that the bill could have important benefits for the clean energy transition but expressing concern over rollbacks to bedrock environmental laws and the rights of tribes. On Friday, the Sierra Club issued a fuller-throated opposition.

“As currently drafted, this bill will hand more power to the executive branch, erode democratic norms, and cause environmental harm to our water, wildlife, and public health protections far beyond the scope of federal permitting. The Sierra Club cannot support this bill as currently written,” Sierra Club executive director Loren Blackford wrote in a statement Friday.

entries.title: Trump Says an All-Out Return to Iran War Is ‘Highly Unlikely’
entries.summary: The president told CNN that Iran must “sign a very strong agreement” to avoid returning to a larger-scale conflict.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump appeared to dismiss the possibility of returning to an all-out war with Iran, telling CNN’s Jim Sciutto he believes it is “highly unlikely” as long as there is progress through negotiations.

The president said the decision to return to major military conflict between the U.S. and Iran hinges on “whether or not they sign a very strong agreement.”

“Most likely it will not be necessary,” Trump said of continued fighting. “They want to make a deal so badly.”

Trump repeatedly said Iran was “withering away” both financially and militarily on the roughly 20-minute call with Sciutto, CNN reported Sunday, but added that the U.S. forces in the Middle East are prepared to strike at any moment.

“I would, if necessary,” strike them again, Trump said, “but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.”

U.S. and Iranian officials have not had direct talks in months after negotiations this summer failed to reach an agreement to end the war, leaving indirect negotiations as the chief method of communication between the two countries.

Iran sent a new proposal to Washington through Qatari mediators on Thursday, which included a list of seven conditions that the U.S. needs to meet before Iran will agree to any discussions. Some of Iran’s terms include lifting U.S. sanctions and war reparations, Reuters reported last week.

In the days after the midterms, Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have cited the Iran war as a significant factor in Democrats’ sweeping successes across the country.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi urged the U.S. to accept his country’s terms and move forward with Iran’s accelerated plan to end the war, citing the American midterm results.

“American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own,” Araghchi wrote Sunday on X. “Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results.”

Trump announced a temporary pause in U.S. strikes on Iran on Oct. 8, and the ceasefire was supposed to last through the midterms — though limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets resumed shortly before Election Day.

The brief lull in larger-scale military strikes follows several intense campaigns. U.S. forces hit Iranian targets for 13 straight nights in July and launched major attacks on Iranian facilities in September. U.S.-Iranian hostilities have persisted throughout the conflict’s fluctuations, most notably through naval blockades and exchanges of fire in the Strait of Hormuz — leading to severe spikes in global oil prices.

U.S. Central Command’s Adm. Brad Cooper unveiled the Iron Gate Task Force on Saturday to specifically reinforce “the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea." The task force will consist of a mix of approximately 20 civilian and military personnel based in CENTCOM’s Tampa, Florida, headquarters.

Trump has repeatedly asserted that Iran must not have a nuclear weapon, and U.S. military efforts do not appear to have strayed from that course. On Friday, CENTCOM announced $20 million compensation and “possible relocation” for individuals that provide tips about Iran’s nuclear program “including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above.”

entries.title: The Commanders Lose All Steam in a 20-13 Loss to the Rams
entries.summary: After a strong start, Washington had no answers for Los Angeles' star power in the second half.
entries.content:
Entering Sunday's meeting with the Rams, there is no doubt the Commanders (2-5-1) knew they would have to stop Los Angeles wideout Puka Nacua. He was, arguably, the one player Washington had to eliminate on a banged-up Los Angeles offense.

And yet, Nacua accounted for nearly half of his team’s output on Sunday, catching 14 passes for 150 yards and a touchdown in the Rams' 20-13 win over Washington in Landover.

Whenever a big play was needed, the fourth-year pro delivered. All the Commanders could do was watch.

Washington's defense limited nearly everyone else — no running back had more than 60 yards on the ground and no other receiver totaled more than 20. But it didn't matter, in part because the Commanders' offense was nonexistent.

A six-play, 80-yard touchdown drive in the first quarter, boosted by a 45-yard screen pass from Jayden Daniels to Rachaad White, was the only real highlight of the day for the unit. Following that scoring drive, the Commanders didn’t get past the 50-yard line again until late in the third quarter.

"We have not nailed our complementary football, and I will keep saying that until we do," coach Dan Qunn said after the game.

Daniels finished 24 of 35 for 274 yards and a touchdown, but Washington totaled just 60 yards on the ground. Van Jefferson led the pass-catchers with five catches for 58 yards.

The Rams pass-rushing duo of Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett — playing in their first game together — lived up to their billing: Garrett finished with three sacks, while Donald disrupted the run game.

The lack of an offensive output spoiled a solid performance by the Washington defense. Even with Nacua doing his thing, the Rams didn’t convert on a third down until the third quarter, and safety Nick Cross had his best game of the season: eight total tackles (one for loss), three passes defended, an interception and a fumble recovery.

A late attempt to tie the game died on a fourth-and-17 with just under two minutes left. After a quick defensive stop, the offense got one more chance. A 41-yard bomb from Daniels to Stefon Diggs generated some excitement, but the drive stalled soon after.

The Commanders will head to New York on Thursday to face the division-leading Giants (5-2-1). After the game, Daniels said that his team is running out of time to get things right.

"Next week is a must-win," he said.
